analysis.one_liner: Protects workers' right to discuss their wages without employer retaliation.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2000.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it illegal for employers to fire or punish workers for asking about, discussing, or disclosing wages, and to bar companies from imposing wage confidentiality policies on employees. It included a narrow exception letting employers keep payroll and HR staff from sharing other employees' wage data. It never advanced past a committee referral before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially women and others affected by pay gaps, gain the legal ability to find out whether they are being paid less than coworkers for the same work without risking their jobs. Under the bill, a violation would be enforced the same way as other Fair Labor Standards Act violations, giving workers a way to sue.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for an employer to discharge or discriminate against an employee for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, or for participating in an investigation or proceeding under the provision.
Prohibits employers from making or enforcing written or oral confidentiality policies that stop employees from discussing wages, closing off a common tool used to keep pay secret.
Enforces the new protections through the Fair Labor Standards Act's existing violation, penalty, and enforcement provisions (sections 15, 16, and 17), so workers would have a private legal remedy.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost: they could no longer enforce wage secrecy policies covering ordinary workers and would face legal exposure if they retaliated against employees who talk about pay. Pay transparency tends to surface and narrow pay gaps, which means higher wage bills for companies that were paying some workers less than others doing the same job.

drawbacks.text: The bill carries legal risk for employers: any discharge or discipline connected to wage discussions could become the basis for a lawsuit under the Fair Labor Standards Act's enforcement provisions.

The bill does allow employers to keep confidentiality rules for employees who regularly handle other workers' pay data in their jobs (such as payroll and HR staff), so full wage transparency within a workplace would not be automatic.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are real but indirect: pay transparency does not by itself raise anyone's wage, but it lets workers detect unequal pay and enforce existing equal-pay rights, which matters most for women and others historically underpaid. The cost falls on employers, who lose a cheap and effective way to suppress wage information and litigation leverage. The carve-out for payroll staff is a reasonable limit, though enforcement would depend entirely on individual workers being willing to sue.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Jim Jeffords introduced the Wage Awareness Protection Act on July 27, 2000, with Senator Max Baucus, Senator John Edwards, and Senator William Roth as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to prohibit employer retaliation and confidentiality policies relating to disclosure of employee wages.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they can continue enforcing wage confidentiality policies and are not exposed to new retaliation claims under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Workers who wanted a federal right to discuss pay without fear of firing got nothing during this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont (HELP Committee chair), bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on July 27, 2000.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was split across party lines: Republican Senator Jim Jeffords sponsored the bill, with one more Republican (Roth) and two Democrats (Baucus and Edwards) as cosponsors.

industries.industry: Employers (general business, especially retail, food service, and other large low-wage workforces)
industries.note: Wage confidentiality policies are a common tool for keeping pay differences hidden, which lowers the chance workers will demand raises or bring equal-pay claims. The bill would have taken that tool away and created legal exposure for retaliating against workers who discuss pay.

industries.industry: Human resources and payroll functions within employers
industries.note: The bill would have limited HR and payroll staff from disclosing coworkers' wages in the course of their jobs, but employees would still keep the right to disclose their own wages.
